title: Mammoth Cave saltpeter
summary: In the early 1800s, enslaved African American men dug Mammoth Cave's nitrate-rich dirt to make saltpeter for gunpowder, and their works still stand inside.
bodyMarkdown:
Before Mammoth Cave drew tourists, it was a mine. In the early 1800s workers dug its dry cave dirt to make saltpeter, the main ingredient of gunpowder. Most of that work was done by enslaved African American men, and the remains of their labor still stand inside the Historic Entrance.

## Why the dirt mattered

The National Park Service article [From Dirt to Gunpowder](https://www.nps.gov/articles/000/saltpetre-mining.htm) explains that thousands of years of bat guano made the cave soil rich in calcium nitrate. Mixed with high-potassium materials, it could be turned into potassium nitrate, or saltpeter.

Sources frame the wartime demand differently. The Park Service points to the British blockade of eastern ports, which made imported gunpowder hard to get. An account of [Mammoth Cave National Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mammoth_Cave_National_Park) points to the Embargo Act of 1807, which banned foreign trade.

## Owners

The land around the Historic Entrance was first surveyed in the name of Valentine Simon. One account dates the survey to 1798. A Park Service [Teaching with Historic Places lesson](https://www.nps.gov/articles/000/upload/TwHP-Lessons_35mammoth.pdf) dates it to 1799.

In July 1812 Charles Wilkins and Philadelphia investor Hyman Gratz bought the cave. The National Park Service lesson says the cave was first called Mammoth Cave on a map produced in 1810, made to show where the saltpeter deposits lay.

## The mining works

Workers carried cave dirt to wooden vats and soaked it with water. The Park Service's page on the [Saltpetre Vats in the Rotunda](https://www.nps.gov/places/saltpetre-vats-rotunda.htm) describes three large square boxes and the scaffolding of a holding tank. Pipes made of hollowed tulip poplar logs carried water from a waterfall at the entrance. The lesson says leaching vats stood in both the Rotunda and Booth's Amphitheater.

The nitrate solution was collected and pumped by hand through another wooden pipeline back to the surface, where it was mixed with wood ash, and sometimes ox blood, to make saltpeter.

## Enslaved miners

The lesson and another account both put the workforce at about 70 enslaved African Americans. The Park Service adds that many were leased from nearby states and worked long hours in poor conditions. They also built many of the cave's first trails, clearing rocks and laying flat stones so carts pulled by oxen and donkeys could pass.

## How much

The [Grokipedia entry on Mammoth Cave National Park](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mammoth_Cave_National_Park) gives two figures. It says operations produced about 400,000 pounds of saltpeter in all, and about 115,000 pounds in 1814 alone.

## After the war

The war ended in 1815, demand fell, and mining stopped. As early as 1816, the Park Service says, travelers came to see the cave instead. A steel door was installed in Houchin's Narrows, and visitors bought tickets. In 1838 the Gratz brothers sold the cave to Franklin Gorin, who ran it as a tourist attraction with enslaved guides.

## Kentucky today

The vats and wooden pipes, now more than 200 years old, are preserved by the cave's environment. Visitors can see them just inside the Historic Entrance. A smaller mine of the same era is told in [Saltpeter Cave at Carter Caves](/stories/saltpeter-cave-at-carter-caves/).
